huperzine-a.summary: Club-moss extract that height-maxxers use hoping to raise growth hormone for added height; it is a prescription Alzheimer's drug in China and a supplement elsewhere.

quick.overview:
Huperzine A is an alkaloid from Chinese club moss. In height-maxxing circles it is used for the added-height payoff people want from higher growth hormone, often alongside growth-hormone-boosting routines.

The theory is that blocking acetylcholinesterase lowers somatostatin, the brake on growth hormone, so more is released. Clinical research has studied it for Alzheimer's disease and cognition, not height, and some forum users dispute the somatostatin link.
quick.how: People take it as an oral supplement, usually as one piece of a wider height or sleep-and-recovery stack, and often alongside growth-hormone-boosting habits. It is also sold as a nootropic. Users who try it for height typically run it over weeks to months and judge results by how they feel and by growth-plate status rather than any measured outcome.
quick.risks: Reported side effects include mild nausea, dizziness and insomnia. It can interact with other cholinesterase inhibitors and anticholinergic drugs. It is a prescription drug for Alzheimer's in China and sold as a supplement in the US. Growth plates close after puberty, so height gains are not expected in adults.

angle.text: Huperzine A is a club-moss extract that height-maxxers take hoping to lower somatostatin, raise growth hormone and gain height. It is approved for Alzheimer's in China and sold as a nootropic; its research is in cognition, and forum users disagree about the height theory.

bacopa-monnieri.summary: Ayurvedic brahmi herb taken as a memory and stress nootropic to support study and focus; trials are small and results vary by extract.

quick.overview:
Bacopa monnieri, or brahmi, is a wetland herb used for centuries in Ayurvedic medicine for memory and learning. People take it for sharper focus, steadier stress, and better study sessions.

Its bacosides show antioxidant and neurotransmitter effects in lab and animal work. Small human trials in healthy adults and older people have looked at memory, with results that vary by extract type; no trial has looked at appearance.
quick.how: Taken as a daily oral supplement, usually an extract, and often stacked with other nootropics for study or work. Users generally report that effects build over weeks of consistent use rather than immediately, and many take it with food.
quick.risks: The most commonly reported effects are nausea, looser stools and stomach upset. In 2019 the US FDA sent warning letters to supplement makers over disease claims and stated that no Bacopa product is approved for medical use.

angle.text: Bacopa, or brahmi, is taken as a memory herb for study performance and calmer stress, which people link to better days overall. Small trials have studied memory, and its use in looksmaxxing circles is as a general nootropic.

ginkgo-biloba.summary: Ginkgo leaf extract taken for memory and circulation as a general nootropic; large reviews have not found conclusive benefit and it can interact with blood thinners.

quick.overview:
Ginkgo biloba extract comes from the leaves of the ginkgo tree and is one of the best-known herbal supplements for memory and blood flow. People take it for mental performance and general circulation support.

Extracts contain flavonoids and terpene lactones, studied for antioxidant and blood-flow effects. Large reviews have not found conclusive cognitive benefit in healthy people, while a standardised extract is registered in the EU as a herbal medicine for mild dementia.
quick.how: Used as a daily oral capsule or tablet of standardised leaf extract, often as a background nootropic in recovery or study routines. Users commonly take it for weeks to months.
quick.risks: Reported effects include stomach upset, headache, dizziness and bleeding risk, and interactions with warfarin and antiplatelet drugs are a concern. Ginkgolic acids can cause allergic skin reactions, and many raw seeds can cause ginkgotoxin poisoning. IARC classified the extract as possibly carcinogenic in 2016.

angle.text: Ginkgo is taken for memory and circulation, and users fold it into recovery and study routines for sharper mental performance. Large reviews have not found conclusive cognitive benefit, and appearance outcomes have not been studied.

vinpocetine.summary: Periwinkle-derived compound taken for memory and focus; a prescription drug in parts of Europe and a US supplement, with an FDA pregnancy warning.

quick.overview:
Vinpocetine is a semi-synthetic derivative of vincamine, an alkaloid from lesser periwinkle. People take it as a nootropic for memory and focus, on the idea that it supports blood flow in the brain.

It was developed in Hungary and has been used for decades in parts of Europe and Asia for cerebrovascular disorders. Reviews note the evidence does not fully support benefit in dementia or stroke, and it has not been studied for appearance.
quick.how: Taken as an oral supplement, usually as part of a nootropic stack for study or work. Users typically describe it as a short-term focus aid and take it alongside other cognition supplements.
quick.risks: Reported effects include flushing, nausea, dizziness, dry mouth, headache, heartburn and blood-pressure changes. The FDA warned in 2019 that it may cause miscarriage or harm fetal development, so pregnancy is a firm no-go. US regulators regard it as an unapproved new drug.

angle.text: Vinpocetine is taken by people chasing better memory and focus, on the idea that it supports blood flow in the brain. It is a prescription drug in parts of Europe, and its research is in dementia and stroke rather than appearance.

sulbutiamine.summary: Fat-soluble thiamine (B1) derivative prescribed for fatigue in France and sold as a supplement for energy and motivation.

quick.overview:
Sulbutiamine is a synthetic compound made of two thiamine (vitamin B1) units, designed to be fat-soluble so it enters the body and brain more readily. People take it for more energy, motivation and mental stamina, which supports staying consistent with training and routines.

Servier has marketed it in France since 1973 as Arcalion for asthenia. After absorption it is reduced to thiamine, and rodent and cell studies show it raises thiamine phosphate levels, including in brain tissue. Human data come from small studies, including an uncontrolled trial in multiple sclerosis fatigue.
quick.how: Taken as an oral supplement, typically in the morning, and used as an energy or mental-stamina aid. Many users take it only occasionally rather than every day because of tolerance.
quick.risks: Trials mostly report headache and stomach discomfort at high doses. Daily use can lead to tolerance and paradoxical drowsiness. Other reports include diarrhea, insomnia, constipation and vertigo. It is not FDA-approved as a drug and appears on a US Department of Defense prohibited supplement list.

angle.text: Sulbutiamine is taken for less fatigue and more energy and motivation, which helps people keep up their training and routines. It is prescribed for asthenia in France; human data are sparse and no appearance outcome has been studied.

pyritinol.summary: Vitamin B6 disulfide analog approved in several European countries for dementia-related impairment and sold as a US nootropic for memory and focus.

quick.overview:
Pyritinol is a semi-synthetic compound made by linking two vitamin B6 molecules, produced by Merck in 1961. People take it as a nootropic for memory, focus and mental performance.

It is approved in several European countries for chronically impaired brain function in dementia syndromes, and in the US it has been sold as a supplement since the early 1990s. Human trials are mostly old and small with mixed results, and none address appearance.
quick.how: Taken orally as a nootropic supplement, usually as part of a study or work stack. Users generally treat it as a short-run cognitive aid.
quick.risks: Common effects are nausea and headache; mild skin allergy is rare. Case reports describe severe cholestatic hepatitis in patients on several drugs, acute pancreatitis, a photoallergic eruption and induced pemphigus. It is not recognised as a drug by the FDA.

angle.text: Pyritinol is taken as a nootropic for sharper memory and focus. It is approved in several European countries for dementia-related impairment, and its trials are mostly older cognition studies, with nothing on appearance.

meclofenoxate-centrophenoxine.summary: DMAE-ester nootropic with an anti-aging reputation from 1970s elderly-memory studies and a mouse-lifespan report; no studies on skin.

quick.overview:
Meclofenoxate (centrophenoxine) is an ester of DMAE and 4-chlorophenoxyacetic acid, promoted as an anti-aging nootropic. People take it hoping for sharper cognition and a younger-looking, healthier ageing profile.

Its reputation rests on findings about lipofuscin (age pigment) in the brain, a reported 26.5 percent lifespan increase in mice, and a 1977 study that reported improved memory-test performance in elderly patients. It is classed as a cholinergic nootropic. No studies have looked at skin.
quick.how: Sold as a supplement in the US and as a prescription drug under names such as Lucidril in Japan and parts of Europe. Users take it orally, often as part of an anti-aging or nootropic routine over weeks to months.
quick.risks: Rare effects include insomnia, dizziness, restlessness, tremor, depression, nausea and headache. It is not FDA-approved, is prescription-only in places such as Germany and Japan, and Brazil listed it as a controlled substance in 2023.

angle.text: Centrophenoxine is promoted as an anti-aging nootropic, and people tie that to staying sharp and looking younger. The reputation comes from 1970s elderly-memory studies and a mouse-lifespan report; no study has examined skin.

bromantane.summary: Russian stimulant-anxiolytic taken for motivation and lower stress, which users link to better training drive; human data are small and mostly Russian-language.

quick.overview:
Bromantane is a Russian-developed adamantane drug, sold there as Ladasten for neurasthenia. People use it for motivation, calmer social stress and a steadier training drive, and some claim it also lifts testosterone for physique gains.

Animal research reports it increases the enzymes that make dopamine rather than mainly blocking its reuptake. Most human evidence is from Russian-language studies; the testosterone and physique claims circulate in forums and have not been tested in published human trials.
quick.how: Used as an oral nootropic, typically for motivation and stress resilience during demanding training or work periods. It is often discussed alongside recovery routines.
quick.risks: Russian studies report few side effects (about 3% of patients in one large study), but long-term data in healthy users are lacking. It is prescription-only in Russia, not FDA-approved, and banned by WADA since 1997, which matters for tested athletes.

angle.text: Bromantane is taken for motivation and lower social stress, with users linking that to better training drive and physique results, and some claim it raises testosterone. Human data are small and mostly Russian-language, and the physique claims are anecdotal.

phosphatidylserine.summary: Membrane phospholipid sold for memory and exercise recovery, which lifters link to training harder; trials are mainly in cognition.

quick.overview:
Phosphatidylserine (PS) is a fat-like molecule found in every cell membrane and concentrated in the brain. Supplements are sold for memory and, in sports products, for recovery from exercise stress, which lifters tie to training harder and keeping progress going.

PS helps anchor signalling proteins in neuron membranes. Human trials have studied cognition in older adults, children with ADHD and athletes; none examine appearance. The FDA allowed a qualified health claim in 2003 noting the evidence is limited and preliminary.
quick.how: Taken as an oral supplement, now usually soy-derived, often in recovery or evening stacks and in sports products. Users typically take it daily over weeks.
quick.risks: A 2002 safety report found a daily regimen safe in elderly people. Supplements are lightly regulated products, and the 2003 FDA health claim carries a disclaimer that the evidence is limited. EFSA concluded in 2010 that cause and effect had not been established for several claims.

angle.text: Phosphatidylserine is taken as a recovery supplement that lifters link to a lower exercise stress response and harder training. Trials have studied it mainly for cognition, and none are on appearance.

dimethylaminoethanol-dmae.summary: Ingredient in skin-firming creams for a tighter, smoother look, also sold as an oral nootropic; no human trial isolates its skin effect.

quick.overview:
DMAE is an amino alcohol that appears in some skin-care products marketed for firming and improving skin tone. People use it hoping for tighter-looking skin and fewer visible wrinkles.

It is mainly an industrial chemical, and its bitartrate salt is sold as an oral nootropic. No mechanism for skin firming is documented, and animal work cited for it concerns memory. The only registered human study found involving a DMAE skin product tested a multi-ingredient combination.
quick.how: Used as a topical cream or serum ingredient, usually in a daily face-care routine, or as an oral supplement. Users of firming products typically apply them for weeks before judging results.
quick.risks: The pure industrial liquid is flammable and corrosive and carries hazard warnings. Safety data for cosmetic or supplement use in people are limited.

angle.text: DMAE is an ingredient in skin-firming creams marketed for a tighter, smoother look, and is also sold as an oral nootropic. The only registered human study found tested a multi-ingredient product.

methylsulfonylmethane-msm.summary: Sulfur supplement taken for softer skin, stronger hair and nails, and comfortable joints; a few small skin trials exist.

quick.overview:
MSM is a sulfur compound found in trace amounts in foods and sold as a supplement for joints, skin, hair and nails. People take it for smoother, healthier-looking skin, better hair and nails, and joints that stay comfortable for training.

The idea is that it supplies sulfur to skin and hair tissue. Small randomised trials of skin and hair outcomes report improved wrinkles and hydration, though they are small and short. Forum claims about lightening skin or eye colour and preserving height appear only in anecdote.
quick.how: Taken orally as a daily powder or capsule, and also used in topical products. Users commonly combine it with collagen, vitamin C or joint supplements and judge results over several weeks.
quick.risks: Animal studies suggest very low toxicity, and a branded form received an FDA non-objection letter for GRAS status. It has no approved medical uses, and long-term human data are limited.

angle.text: MSM is taken for softer skin, stronger hair and nails, and comfortable joints for training, on the idea that it supplies sulfur to those tissues. A few small skin trials exist; the claims about lightening skin or eyes and preserving height rest on anecdote.

hydroxycitric-acid-hca.summary: Garcinia-derived acid sold as a fat blocker for a leaner body; trials report small short-term weight differences.

quick.overview:
HCA is the main acid in the rind of the Garcinia cambogia fruit, sold as a fat-loss supplement and often found in fat-burner blends. People take it to store less fat and get leaner.

In the lab it inhibits ATP citrate lyase, an enzyme that supplies building blocks for fat synthesis. Human trials have measured weight rather than visible leanness: a 1998 JAMA trial found no advantage over placebo, and a 2011 meta-analysis found a small short-term difference of uncertain relevance.
quick.how: Taken orally as capsules before meals, usually alongside a calorie deficit and training, or as one ingredient in a fat-burner blend. Users judge results over several weeks.
quick.risks: A meta-analysis reported about twice the rate of gastrointestinal side effects. It is considered contraindicated in colitis or inflammatory bowel disease, and reviews of liver injury list Garcinia products.

angle.text: HCA from Garcinia cambogia is taken to block fat storage and get leaner. The mechanism comes from lab enzyme data, and human trials have measured weight rather than visible leanness, reporting small short-term differences.

hydroxycut.summary: Mass-market caffeine and coffee-extract fat burner used while cutting to get leaner; a 2009 FDA warning and recall followed liver-injury reports.

quick.overview:
Hydroxycut is a mainstream fat-burner brand launched in 2002 by MuscleTech and now sold by Iovate. People use it during cutting phases to feel more energised, curb appetite and get leaner alongside diet and exercise.

Formulas have changed from ephedra-era versions to current blends built on caffeine and robusta coffee extract (chlorogenic acids). The company cites two studies of its coffee extract, and critics have said independent evidence for the finished products is lacking.
quick.how: Taken as capsules or powders during a cut, usually with a calorie deficit and training, often before workouts for the energy boost. Users typically cycle it over a diet phase.
quick.risks: In 2009 the FDA warned consumers to stop using Hydroxycut products after reports of liver damage and at least one death, and the maker recalled them. Case series describe liver injury, and stimulant versions carry caffeine effects such as jitteriness and poor sleep.

angle.text: Hydroxycut is a mass-market caffeine fat burner that people use during cutting phases for energy and appetite control on the way to a leaner look. Current formulas centre on caffeine and robusta coffee extract; the evidence cited comes mostly from manufacturer-linked studies.

dexatrim.summary: Long-running diet-pill brand used as an appetite suppressant and energy aid; it dropped PPA after the FDA's 2000 action and now sells caffeine and green-tea blends.

quick.overview:
Dexatrim is an over-the-counter diet pill brand sold since the 1970s. People use it to eat less and keep energy up while dieting, to lose weight and body fat.

The original ingredient was phenylpropanolamine (PPA), an appetite-reducing sympathomimetic, removed after regulatory action in 2000. Current versions are blends of caffeine, green tea extract and other botanicals. No trials of current formulations were found, and the individual ingredients have been studied with limited results.
quick.how: Taken as capsules during a diet, usually timed around meals to curb appetite and lift energy, and combined with calorie control and exercise.
quick.risks: PPA-era use was linked in case reports and a Yale study to hemorrhagic stroke, heart injury and neurological effects. Current stimulant blends carry caffeine-type effects such as insomnia and palpitations, and labels advise caution with heart conditions and pregnancy.

angle.text: Dexatrim is a long-running diet-pill brand used to blunt appetite and add energy while cutting, leading to lower calorie intake and fat loss. Current versions are caffeine and green-tea blends, and no trials of the branded formulas were found.

cortislim.summary: Cortisol-themed weight-loss supplement marketed for trimming stress-linked belly fat; advertising drew an FTC action and no trials were found.

quick.overview:
CortiSlim is a brand of weight-loss supplements marketed around lowering the stress hormone cortisol. People bought it hoping to lose weight, especially around the midsection.

The marketing idea was that stress-related cortisol promotes fat storage and that herbal blends of magnolia bark, green tea and banana leaf extracts could modulate cortisol, appetite and blood sugar. No studies were found showing the product changes cortisol or body weight, and the FTC found its claims of supporting research to be false.
quick.how: Taken as pills in a diet or stress-management routine, usually alongside calorie control. The brand was sold by CortiSlim International and earlier by Window Rock Enterprises, and was acquired in 2008.
quick.risks: Ingredients include bitter orange (synephrine), green tea extract and vanadyl sulfate, each with its own safety considerations. The marketing was the subject of FTC action and the original marketer went bankrupt.

angle.text: CortiSlim was marketed to people wanting to lose midsection fat by controlling cortisol. No published trials test the product, and its advertising drew an FTC action.

metabolife.summary: Best-selling ephedra-and-caffeine fat burner of its era; ended by cardiovascular safety reports, litigation, the 2004 ephedra ban and bankruptcy.

quick.overview:
Metabolife 356 was a top-selling diet supplement combining ephedra and caffeine, sold from the mid-1990s by Metabolife International. Dieters used it for more energy, less appetite and faster weight loss for a leaner look.

Ephedra's alkaloids and caffeine stimulate the sympathetic nervous system, raising heart rate and metabolic rate and suppressing appetite. The ephedra-caffeine combination has been studied for short-term weight loss. It is documented here as a historical example.
quick.how: It was sold through a customer-driven distribution model and used during diets for energy and appetite control. It is no longer available in its ephedra form after the 2004 US ban.
quick.risks: A 2004 randomized trial found cardiovascular effects, and case reports describe heart attack, stroke, psychosis and diabetic ketoacidosis. Ephedra supplements have been banned in the US since 2004, and the company filed for bankruptcy in 2005 after adverse-event reports, a congressional investigation and litigation.

angle.text: Metabolife 356 was the best-selling fat burner of its era, taken by dieters for energy and appetite control on the way to a leaner look. Its ephedra-caffeine combination has been studied for short-term weight loss; it is documented here as a historical example after the federal ephedra ban.

chromium-nicotinate.summary: Niacin-bound chromium supplement sold for fat loss, muscle gain and blood sugar control; trials of chromium forms show no reliable body-composition benefit.

quick.overview:
Chromium nicotinate is trace-mineral chromium bound to niacin, sold in supplements marketed for weight loss, muscle building and blood sugar. People take it for fewer cravings, better nutrient use and a leaner, more muscular look.

Chromium has been proposed to enhance insulin signaling, possibly through a chromium-binding peptide. Reviews of chromium supplements report no reliable evidence for body-weight effects, EFSA found evidence insufficient for body-weight claims, and a trial of chromium nicotinate in type 2 diabetes found no effect on insulin sensitivity. Most research covers picolinate rather than nicotinate.
quick.how: Taken orally as a daily supplement, often in multivitamin or fat-loss and body-composition stacks, alongside diet and training. Users judge results over weeks to months.
quick.risks: Little evidence of toxicity at typical amounts; rare allergic reactions, headache, insomnia and kidney or liver reports exist, mostly with picolinate. It may interact with medicines, including insulin.

angle.text: Chromium nicotinate is taken for fat loss, muscle gain and blood sugar control, on the idea that chromium improves how the body handles carbohydrate. Trials of chromium forms have measured body composition directly, with mixed results.

policosanol.summary: Sugarcane-wax alcohol mixture sold for cholesterol and metabolic health; lipid results are debated and no studies address body fat or looks.

quick.overview:
Policosanol is a mixture of long-chain waxy alcohols, chiefly octacosanol, extracted from plant waxes such as sugarcane. It is sold as a cholesterol supplement and appears in metabolism-focused stacks that people use for general health.

It was developed commercially in Cuba in the 1990s, where trials reported lower cholesterol. Groups outside Cuba have not reproduced those results, though a 2018 meta-analysis reported improved lipid profiles. Cell studies suggest it may suppress cholesterol synthesis via AMP-kinase. No studies address body fat or appearance.
quick.how: Taken as a daily oral supplement, usually as part of a cholesterol or metabolic-health routine and sometimes included in fat-loss stacks through the general-health link.
quick.risks: A 2005 meta-analysis described it as well tolerated. EFSA rejected a cholesterol health claim in 2011.

angle.text: Policosanol is a sugarcane-wax supplement used for cholesterol, and people include it in metabolism and fat-loss stacks for general metabolic health. Lipid results are debated, and no studies address body fat or appearance.

red-yeast-rice.summary: Fermented rice containing natural lovastatin, used for cholesterol and long-term cardiovascular health; contents vary between products.

quick.overview:
Red yeast rice is rice fermented with Monascus mold, used for centuries in Chinese food and medicine and now sold for cholesterol. It appears in longevity routines as part of keeping the heart and body healthy over decades.

It contains monacolin K, identical to lovastatin, which inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme that makes cholesterol. Randomized trials report lower LDL cholesterol, and a large Chinese trial of the extract Xuezhikang in post-heart-attack patients reported fewer coronary events. It has not been studied for appearance outcomes.
quick.how: Taken as a daily oral supplement, usually as part of a cholesterol or longevity routine, often as an alternative some people consider alongside diet changes.
quick.risks: Reported effects resemble statins, including muscle and liver problems. Monacolin content varies and some products contain citrinin; EFSA in 2018 found no safe intake for monacolin preparations, and the FDA treats products with substantial monacolin K as drugs.

angle.text: Red yeast rice is taken for cholesterol and appears in longevity routines as part of keeping the body healthy over decades. Its cholesterol effect has been studied in trials; it is not used for a direct appearance outcome.

fucoidan.summary: Brown-seaweed sulfated sugar sold as a longevity and skin supplement; lab and animal results are plentiful, human appearance trials have not been run.

quick.overview:
Fucoidan is a family of sulfated polysaccharides from brown seaweeds such as kombu and wakame. It is sold as a supplement and cosmetic ingredient in longevity lines, and people take it for healthy ageing and younger-looking skin.

Cell and animal studies report anti-inflammatory, antiviral and antioxidant activity, tied to its fucose backbone and sulfate groups. Human trials are small and mostly address medical conditions; none test a cosmetic or appearance outcome. Products vary widely in seaweed source and extraction.
quick.how: Taken as an oral supplement or extract, daily, as a general-purpose marine addition to a longevity stack. It also appears as an ingredient in some topical products.
quick.risks: Evidence for human safety is limited and product quality varies. It shows anticoagulant activity in lab tests, and seaweed products can carry variable iodine and metal content. It is not approved as a drug in any country.

angle.text: Fucoidan is a seaweed extract sold in longevity circles for healthy ageing and younger-looking skin. Most findings come from cell and animal studies on inflammation and skin biology; human trials on appearance have not been run.
